title: The Nine Wells — on the Keel
caption: The close ground of the Keel's hot springs, five leagues short of the Hearthseat, drawn in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, when the road came up frozen hard enough for a cart and the steam stood a hand high over the water. At the centre the counting stone holds nine cups cut into one stone: five worn smooth with thumbs and open, named in the well-ledger as the child's lip, the bakehouse well, the stone-warmer's, the milk well and the last open with its copper bit unspent; four stopped with lead, six through nine, whose length the warming-song leaves as a silence and a clerk puts a round nought against. The dish stands on the whitewashed lip with lime bloom worked into its grain, warm-stone grit is ground small between the cups, the grey from the Last Day lies on the fifth lip, and a reader holds his palm flat to the stone while the woman who keeps it draws water and a clerk come up from Slate Row enters a nought. Beyond, four covered springs bear a stone and a ring of cold iron with no name cut upon them, and the fifth, sealed in Y.H. 618, keeps the keeper's hanged account carried forward. The Hearth Road runs up to the Hearthseat and down to Greybank; a south way goes by report toward the Empty Cantons. Cartouche with a starred border, compass, a league scale, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the two counts that do not agree --- four stopped on the stone, five sealed in the books --- the reeve's claim that the fifth spring lies under the Cantons, the keeper with no licence to draw a map, the bit put in and not taken out, and the struck line at the foot in a hand nobody will own: five were left open by a hand, four were stopped by another, and the steam does not tell which hand was kinder. An engraved key on a nail in a wool sleeve sits in the margin.
